text: Given the unprecedented pace of coastal erosion, should governments continue investing in mitigation alone, or is it time to prioritize adaptive resilience instead? For decades, climate policy focused almost exclusively on mitigation, reducing emissions to prevent temperatures from crossing dangerous thresholds. Yet as rising seas encroach upon low-lying communities and extreme weather grows more frequent, many experts now argue that vulnerability itself must be addressed directly, rather than treated as a secondary concern. Sustainable infrastructure, designed to withstand flooding and heat rather than merely resist it temporarily, has become central to this proactive shift. Coastal cities are fortifying seawalls, while others are drafting contingency plans for displacement long before disaster forces evacuation. Critics warn that without such foresight, delayed action will only exacerbate future costs, jeopardizing both economies and human lives. Nevertheless, resources remain limited, and every dollar spent fortifying infrastructure is one not spent reducing emissions, a trade-off with no universally viable solution. Notwithstanding this tension, most researchers agree that resilience and mitigation are not competing strategies but complementary ones. Consequently, the most effective climate policy increasingly combines both: cutting emissions today while simultaneously preparing communities to adapt to changes that, however unwelcome, can no longer be avoided.
